where: rewrite/spec/packaging/sandbox-needs.md (T1); item 41 of topics/platform-proven-2.md; rewrite/plans/step-3/survey.md (admission) and ORDER.md rule 11 (flush); rewrite/plans/step-4/delivery.md D7 and ORDER.md rule 7; rewrite/plans/step-5/agents.md M2
problem: sandbox-needs.md listed write access to .factory/ and .worktrees/ but not git's own files for a linked worktree. With the Bash sandbox on (--settings {"sandbox":{"enabled":true}}, default mode, Claude Code 2.1.331, a --plugin-dir plugin), every write under .git/worktrees/ from a workflow step's Bash call is refused with 'Operation not permitted': mkdir .git/worktrees/x, touch inside an existing .git/worktrees/<name>/, git add and git commit in an existing linked worktree ('Unable to create .git/worktrees/z/index.lock') and in the .factory mount, and git worktree add. So nothing can be committed in a story worktree, in the integration worktree or in the .factory state mount, and no worktree can be added. A refused 'git worktree add <path> -b <branch>' has already created the branch, and its retry fails with 'a branch named ... already exists'. A commit with the person's global signing on fails too (gpg cannot reach its agent or write its home). Allowed: reads, git branch, git update-ref, mkdir directly under .git/, a main-checkout commit with signing off. No setting that grants the write was shown: excludedCommands ["sh"] did not take the call out of the sandbox. Not probed: the sandbox set in the project's settings file; a write under .git/worktrees/ from a hook or from a detached job worker. Evidence: rewrite/spike/probes-round-4/CHECK.md (q8-sandbox/s4b.jsonl; reruns D and E2).
proposed_resolution: sandbox-needs.md gains two rows: write access to .git/worktrees/ and, where commits are signed, the gpg home and its agent socket; T1's doctor tests the first by taking the index lock of an existing linked worktree (the .factory mount's), not by adding a worktree. Until an allowance is shown to work, a factory run needs the Bash sandbox off (platform.md, 'Headless runs'); whether that becomes the deployment default is the person's decision. Every unit whose git call is refused this way reports it with a cause that names the sandbox and undoes nothing, so the next run finishes: records' flush (state failed), the survey's worktree library (WorktreeError not_permitted; a branch left without its worktree is reused), delivery (refused), and a builder agent's commit (blocked, kind environment).

where: rewrite/spec/topics/long-commands.md; the G1 open probe in rewrite/plans/step-3/RESOLUTIONS.md; items 43 and 6 of the platform record; rewrite/plans/step-5/agents.md M3 and the clerk
problem: The design worded the Bash timeout as a kill ('the tool stops a foreground command', 'a call killed by a timeout'). Observed on Claude Code 2.1.331, macOS, default mode, sandbox off and on: a foreground call past its Bash timeout is not killed at the timeout. It is moved to the background (timedOutAfterMs, a backgroundTaskId, backgroundEndsWithFinalResponse true), and it is killed when the step agent gives its final response (its task output reads '[killed]'). The platform does reap it, at the step's end. The notice the agent reads at the move tells it to wait for the result before its final response and not to start a second copy while the call runs (item 43 quotes it): the opposite of what a job command needs, so an agent told only to run the command again gets two contradicting instructions. A double-forked worker in its own session (fork, setsid, fork) survived that kill and the session's exit and wrote its file about 40 s later, sandbox off and on, so a job outlives its step only because it is detached: detachment is necessary, not a precaution. Linux is untested. Evidence: rewrite/spike/probes-round-4/CHECK.md (reruns C and D); round 4's own legs did not show survival.
proposed_resolution: long-commands.md states the premise as observed: backgrounded at the timeout, killed at the step's final response, the job surviving because its worker is detached. The job record covers what outlives the step. An agent whose call is moved to the background runs the same command again, which re-attaches, and does not wait for or read the background task. Because the platform's notice says the opposite at that moment, the agent is given the rule with its reason (the re-run re-attaches to the job already running and is not a second copy) in the builder methods' common text and the clerk's rules (step 5), and a lint test checks that the sentence is there. The Linux leg stays an open probe (platform.md, open leg 43). E2's eleven-minute gate reads its transcripts: wherever a call shows the backgrounding signature (timedOutAfterMs, a backgroundTaskId), the step's next Bash call is the same command. A run in which no call was moved says that this was not measured.

where: rewrite/spec/topics/spikes.md; the story-ready fixture, E2's first run and the scheduler recipe (step 6, item 25); item 49 of topics/platform-proven-2.md; rewrite/spec/platform.md, 'Headless runs'
problem: A headless main session told to start a named workflow can pass its own inline script instead: the Workflow tool accepts a script field, and the named plugin workflow never runs. Round 4 lost two probe runs to this. Entering through a typed skill that names the workflow does not prevent it: in the check's rerun E the main session, started through the typed skill, still passed an inline script ('return {}'). Seen in the default mode on Claude Code 2.1.331 with a --plugin-dir plugin. Evidence: rewrite/spike/probes-round-4/CHECK.md (rerun E, E-inline-script).
proposed_resolution: A typed skill or command stays the way in, but it is not the check. Every headless driver (the story-ready fixture, E2's first run, scheduler recipes, probe harnesses) verifies that the named workflow ran, by comparing the run record's scriptPath and script with the plugin's file, or a PreToolUse rule refuses a Workflow call that carries script in a driver session. topics/spikes.md names the inline-script shape as the failure this prevents.
